segments.say: Nadia turns into a long, quiet street lined with plane trees, their leaves pasted flat on the wet pavement. She tries to work out what was actually funny about the teapot lid. It wasn't clever. Nobody was hurt. It just landed, with a tiny plop, exactly where it shouldn't have been. Maybe that was it. Maybe it was just so wrong, and so harmless.

People have been trying to explain what makes things funny for a very long time. Philosophers in ancient Greece wrote about it. So did thinkers in the Enlightenment, and psychologists in the twentieth century. Over the years, three big families of ideas have emerged. None of them explains everything, but each catches something true.

They're usually called superiority, relief and incongruity. Superiority theories say we laugh when we feel above someone else, at their mistakes or misfortunes. Relief theories say laughter lets off built-up nervous energy. And incongruity theories say we laugh when something is unexpected, out of place, or doesn't fit the pattern we expected.

show.title: Three classic families of ideas
items: Incongruity: something unexpected or out of place

segments.say: The superiority idea is very old. Plato and Aristotle both wrote about laughter at other people's faults, and the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes, in the seventeenth century, described laughter as a sudden glory at our own advantage over others. There's some truth in it. Mocking laughter exists, and most of us have felt it, or been on the receiving end.

But superiority can't explain everything. Nobody at Nadia's table felt superior to the teapot. Babies laughing at peekaboo aren't gloating. Friends laughing together over a shared memory aren't putting anyone down. Superiority captures one kind of laughter, but it misses the warm, inclusive kind, which, as we've seen, is probably the most common of all.

show.sub: Nobody felt superior to a teapot

segments.say: Relief theories were popular with nineteenth-century thinkers like the philosopher Herbert Spencer, and later with Sigmund Freud. They saw laughter as a way of releasing pent-up nervous energy, like steam escaping from a valve. That catches something real too. Think of the giggles after a near-miss, or the laughter that bursts out when a tense meeting finally ends.

But the specific idea, that nervous energy builds up inside us like steam in a pipe, doesn't really match what we now know about the nervous system. Relief laughter is real, but the steam-valve picture is more of a metaphor than a mechanism. Today's researchers tend to describe it in terms of shifts in mood and attention instead.

show.cap: But the steam idea is shaky
show.sub: The body doesn't store tension like that

segments.say: Incongruity is the idea that has had the longest life in modern research. Thinkers from the philosopher James Beattie in the eighteenth century to modern psychologists have argued that humour depends on noticing a mismatch, something that doesn't fit what we expected, and then, often, making sense of it in a new way. A punchline, in this view, is a sudden, surprising shift.

A small china teapot lid sitting upside down in a bowl of sugar cubes on a wooden table, lit by a candle. It's the scene that started all the laughter. Not clever, not cruel. Just one thing in a place it should never have been, at a moment when everyone was relaxed enough to notice how ridiculous it looked.

show.cap: A teapot lid in a sugar bowl

segments.say: Incongruity seems to catch a lot. But it has a problem too. Plenty of unexpected things aren't funny at all. A sudden loud bang. A stranger in your kitchen. Bad news out of the blue. These are incongruous, but they're frightening or upsetting, not amusing. So there must be another ingredient, something that turns an odd surprise into a funny one.

show.cap: But not every surprise is funny

segments.say: In 2010, two researchers, Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren, proposed a simple answer, which they called the benign violation theory. Something becomes funny, they suggested, when it seems wrong or threatening in some way, a violation, while at the same time seeming okay, safe, or harmless, benign. Both have to be true at once.

show.what: Benign violations: making immoral behavior funny

segments.say: In their studies, people read short scenarios describing small rule-breaking, and rated how funny and how wrong they seemed. Mild violations, ones that were wrong but didn't really hurt anybody, were the ones people most often found amusing. Too harmless, and there was nothing to laugh at. Too harmful, and it stopped being funny and became upsetting.

Put simply: something seems wrong. But it also seems safe. Both at the same time. And if it's too harmless, or too harmful, the laugh disappears. It's a neat idea, and it explains a fair amount, including why tickling works best from a loving parent, and why a joke that's fine among friends can fall flat with strangers.

show.title: The benign violation idea
items: Too harmless or too harmful kills the laugh

segments.say: It's worth saying clearly that no single theory of humour has won. Benign violation has its critics, who argue that it's so broad it can be stretched to fit almost anything. Other researchers focus on different ingredients, like playfulness, or the pleasure of solving a small puzzle. The honest answer is that humour is probably made of several things at once.

Still, the teapot lid fits rather well. A lid in a sugar bowl is wrong. It's out of place, and slightly absurd. But it's also completely harmless. Nobody's hurt, nothing's broken, and the tea will be fine. Add five relaxed friends, a long history of shared jokes and a late-evening mood, and you have, it seems, the perfect conditions.

And notice that the theories still come back to people. Whether something feels safe depends a great deal on who you're with. The same small accident might feel embarrassing in front of your boss, and hilarious in front of old friends. Humour isn't just in the joke. It's in the relationship between everyone who hears it.

That brings Nadia to another thought. Not every laugh at that dinner was the same. There were the helpless laughs at the teapot. But there were also the polite ones, earlier, when someone told a long story about their job. Can people tell the difference between a real laugh and a polite one? It turns out that they can, and surprisingly well.

show.sub: Not all laughs are the same
